newsitem.title: ANTIGUA AND BARBUDA: U.S. embargo dampens Caribbean view of Cuba.
newsitem.headline: U.S. embargo dampens Caribbean view of Cuba.

text.p: Caribbean leaders meeting this week said they intended to deepen trade links with Cuba but they admitted Washington's attempts to isolate the Communist-ruled island would delay any accord.

The bi-annual meeting of the 15-member Caribbean Community took place almost one year after Cuban fighter jets shot down two U.S. civilian planes piloted by Miami-based Cuban exiles staunchly opposed to President Fidel Castro's government.

The Feb. 24 downing of the planes over international waters chilled U.S.-Cuban relations and prompted Washington to tighten U.S. trade sanctions against the island and push its trading partners to do the same.
The Helms-Burton Act passed last year seeks to discourage investment in Cuba by punishing foreign companies deemed to have profited from property confiscated since the 1959 revolution.
The United States is the Caribbean's largest trading partner, with $15 billion in business each year. Washington also remains an important source of aid.

As a result, while Caribbean governments have established normal diplomatic relations with Havana, Caribbean Community leaders said they were reluctant to move much beyond the decision in 1995 to invite Cuba to join the 25-member Association of Caribbean States, which aims to create a free trade area stretching from Mexico to the Bahamas and Venezuela.
"The reality is the politicians don't want to jeopardise their relations with the U.S.," said one official with close ties to Havana, who asked not to be identified by name.
"Save Trinidad, Barbados, and the Dominican Republic, none of these countries has the capacity to export to Cuba at levels that would justify the political risk."
Publicly, officials attending the meeting expressed optimism about the possibility of closer ties with Cuba.

The European Union-funded Caribbean Export Development Agency is preparing to open an office in Havana, and CEDA's trade representative was already at work attempting to find markets in Cuba for Caribbean goods.
A delegation of regional businessmen went to Cuba to attend a trade exposition late last year.

"These companies took advantage of the opportunity presented as you do not have any American companies in Cuba. If (Caribbean firms) get a foot-hold in the market then they have that advantage," CEDA Executive Director Earle Baccus said.
Cuba first raised the issue of a free trade agreement with Caricom in 1995.

"Both sides are studying the possibility of it being established in the near future", said Jose Franscisco Piedra, head of the Caribbean desk in Cuba's foreign affairs ministry and head of the Cuban delegation at the Caricom summit.
Trinidad, which in 1995 exported $40 million worth of goods to Cuba, has gone a step further and is now negotiating its own trade accord with Havana.
"We have joined with numerous others with respect to rejecting the Helms-Burton act," Trinidad's foreign minister Ralph Maraj said. "Trinidad is very enthusiastic about the trade potential in Cuba."
Total trade between Cuba and the wider Caribbean stood at some $300 million last year, most of it petroleum products exported from Trinidad and the Netherland Antilles.

When the Cuba-Caricom joint trade commission last met in Cuba in 1995, "literally every major proposal made by the Cubans was deferred for consideration," the official said. In addition, the commission was to meet annually and while Havana has offered to host a meeting this year, no date has been set.

"The Cubans are becoming visibly annoyed with the slow pace," the official said. Caricom was to have examined the proposal at this summit, but the matter has been defered to the July heads of government meeting in Jamaica.
